newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Politicians' profiles as Lithuanians vote.
newsitem.headline: Politicians' profiles as Lithuanians vote.

text.p: As Lithuanians voted on Sunday in their second parliamentary elections since quitting the Soviet Union, ex-Communist President Algirdas Brazauskas seemed set for a period of co-operation with a right-wing government.
Opinion polls show the Homeland Union party of independence leader and Brazauskas's long-time rival Vytautas Landsbergis is likely to form the largest party in parliament.
The following is a short profile of Brazauskas, along with some other personalities in the election.
President Algirdas Brazauskas, 63, has worked hard to throw off the Communist label and place himself above party politics as a stable figurehead to unite the nation.

The former head of the Lithuanian Communist Party, he saw the writing on the wall for the Soviet Union and declared his party independent from the all-powerful Communist Party of the Soviet Union (CPSU) in 1989.
Since election in 1993, he has stressed the need for economic reforms and pursued a foreign policy aimed at guaranteeing Lithuania's entry into NATO and the European Union.

The broad-shouldered and ruddy former engineer has also tried to get politicians to maintain high standards of behaviour and has not been afraid to step in against his former party, the Lithuanian Democratic Labour Party (LDLP).
He was behind the dismissal earlier this year of former prime minister Adolfus Slezevicius who withdrew his funds from a bank days before it was closed at the start of a banking crisis.
His style is less confrontational than Landsbergis and his Communist "old boy" ties have helped the country's relaxed relations with Russia.
Prime Minister Mindaugas Stanekvicius, 60, is the LDLP's grey-haired avuncular prime minister, brought in as a non-controversial caretaker after the disgrace of Slezevicius.
He has followed the course set by the previous administration without rocking the boat.
He tried to start some reforms in the key energy sector and relations with Western banks have been boosted under his leadership.
Political commentators wonder whether he will have the fight the LDLP needs should it go into opposition.
Gediminas Vagnorius, 39, is another leader of the Homeland Union and was a former prime minister under Landsbergis.
Many back him for the premier's post again if the Homeland Union becomes the largest party in parliament and forms the core of a right-wing wins coaltion.
But his appointment would not be welcomed in the countryside, a key constituency, where the effects of his ideologically-driven decollectivatisation are still being felt.
An economist by profession, he has drawn criticism for proposals which went against the anti-inflation stabilisation programme Lithuania needed after independence.
Algirdas Saudargas, head of the Christian Democrats and a former foreign minister. His party is expected to form a coalition with the Homeland Union after the elections.

Many predict he would be the choice for the next foreign minister although his fierce patriotism and well-aired mistrust of Russia make him a sharp contrast to the less confrontational current Foreign Minister Povilas Gylys.
